title: MHC Class III: C4A/C4B, C2 and Factor B Deficiency
summary: Learn what the MHC class III region contains, how C4A and C4B differ, and how CH50 and AP50 patterns point to C2 or factor B deficiency.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 51 Hits 4, 7, 9, 12 and 13 and Traps 3–4, checked against Deakin 2006, Arnaiz-Villena 2023, Wang 2021, Macedo 2016, El Sissy 2019, Bougeard 2026 and Harris 2012. Discrepancies: the reviewer’s “likely embryonic lethal” for factor B deficiency conflicts with Bougeard 2026 (complete deficiency reported with normal growth and development; register flag rv-factor-b-not-lethal); C4 gene number “2–4, exceptionally up to 6” vs C4A 0–5, C4B 0–4 and a highest total of 7 (Wang 2021) or 2–8 (Macedo 2016) (rv-c4-copy-number); C2 deficiency SLE “20–40%” and “1 in 10,000” vs 10–30% and 1:10,000–20,000 (Macedo 2016) (rv-c2-deficiency-figures); “complotype” is also used now for the whole complement system (Harris 2012) (rv-complotype-scope). Not taught as fact: C4B 5–10× haemolytic activity, 35% with one C4 null allele, C4B*Q0 3.5-fold meningitis risk, C4A*Q0 homozygosity and SLE, SC01 and the ≥3-Mb extended haplotype, HSP70 in class III, “no homozygous factor B deficiency ever described”, C2 as the single most common complement deficiency.

objectives: Name the complement and inflammatory genes of the MHC class III region and its position between class I and class II.
Contrast C4A and C4B by target chemistry, function and blood-group antigens.
Interpret CH50 and AP50 patterns that suggest C2 or factor B deficiency.

scenes.title: Two gaps, one region
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: two patients, both with normal C3 and C4 levels. (1) A woman with a photosensitive rash, arthritis and recurrent pneumococcal pneumonia: CH50 undetectable, AP50 normal. (2) A teenager with meningococcal meningitis: CH50 normal, AP50 undetectable. Question token: “Which class III gene is missing?”

cues.text: Two invented patients, both with normal C3 and C4. The first has a lupus-like rash, arthritis and repeated pneumococcal pneumonia. Her CH50 is undetectable, but AP50 is normal.
The second, a teenager, has meningococcal meningitis. His CH50 is normal, but AP50 is undetectable.
Both missing proteins are encoded side by side on chromosome six. Which genes are they?

props.label: Which class III gene is missing?

scenes.title: The class III region
scenes.altText: Schematic map of the MHC on chromosome 6p21: class I region (telomeric) · class III region · class II region (centromeric). Class III is defined by its position between class I and class II, not by shared function; in humans it spans about 700 kb, holds 61 genes and is the most gene-dense region of the genome. Contents shown: complement genes C4A, C4B, C2 and factor B (CFB); the “inflammatory region” genes TNF and LTA (lymphotoxin alpha). Card: these genes are usually inherited together; the term complotype was coined for these haplotypic combinations of MHC-linked complement gene variants, and is now also used for complement variants across the whole system.

cues.text: The MHC on chromosome six has three regions. Class three sits between class one and class two. It is defined by its position, not by a shared function, and it is the most gene-dense stretch of the human genome.
It holds four complement genes: C4A and C4B, C2, and factor B, written CFB.
It also holds an inflammatory cluster, including the tumour necrosis factor gene, TNF, and lymphotoxin alpha, LTA.

Genes this close are usually inherited together. The term complotype was coined for these combinations of complement gene variants, and is now also used for complement variants across the whole system.

scenes.title: C4A and C4B are not twins
scenes.altText: Two cards. C4A: reacts preferentially with free amino groups (immune complexes); generally carries Rodgers (Rg) blood-group antigens; more efficient at processing immune complexes; acidic, migrates faster on agarose. C4B: binds preferentially to hydroxyl groups; generally carries Chido (Ch) antigens; more efficient at haemolysis. Strip: the two isotypes share >99% sequence identity; four isotype-specific amino acids at positions 1101–1106 (PCPVLD in C4A vs LSPVIH in C4B). Copy-number card: C4A copies 0–5, C4B 0–4, highest total reported 7; most common is two of each; low total C4 copy number and C4 deficiency are strong SLE risk factors (complete C4 deficiency: >75% develop SLE).

cues.text: C4 comes in two isotypes, C4A and C4B. They are more than ninety-nine percent identical, differing at four amino acids in one short stretch, positions 1101 to 1106.

Those few residues change the chemistry. C4A reacts mainly with amino groups, as on immune complexes, and is better at processing them. C4B binds mainly to hydroxyl groups and is more efficient at lysing cells.
They also carry different blood-group antigens: C4A generally carries Rodgers, and C4B generally carries Chido.

Gene number varies: zero to five copies of C4A and zero to four of C4B, most often two of each. Low C4 copy number is a strong lupus risk factor, and most people with complete C4 deficiency develop lupus.

props.label: C4A 0–5 · C4B 0–4 · low copy number → SLE risk

scenes.title: Reading CH50 and AP50
scenes.altText: Pattern table from a French reference-laboratory cohort: CH50 below 10% with normal AP50 → classical pathway deficiency (C1q, C1r, C1s, C4 or C2; C4 is excluded when the C4 level is normal); CH50 normal + AP50 undetectable + normal C3 → alternative pathway component (factor B, factor D or properdin); both undetectable → terminal pathway. C2 card: type I C2 deficiency, a 28-bp deletion causing exon 6 skipping and a premature stop codon, found in about 90% of complete C2 deficiency; homozygous prevalence about 1 in 10,000–20,000 in Western Europeans, over 60% asymptomatic, about 10–30% develop SLE; infections mostly pneumococcal. Factor B card: extremely rare, only a handful of cases, reported with compound heterozygous variants; infections mostly meningococcal or pneumococcal; growth and development not impaired. Hook answers: (1) C2 deficiency; (2) factor B deficiency (confirm by factor B assay and reconstitution).

cues.text: Two screens read the pathways. CH50 below ten percent with normal AP50 means a classical-pathway gap, such as C2. Normal CH50 with absent AP50 and normal C3 means an alternative-pathway component, such as factor B.
C2 deficiency usually comes from one 28 base-pair deletion that skips exon six. Most homozygotes have no symptoms, a minority develop lupus, and infections are mostly pneumococcal.
Complete factor B deficiency is extremely rare. The few reported patients mostly had meningococcal or pneumococcal infections, and the deficiency does not impair growth or development.
So the first patient most likely lacks C2, and the second lacks factor B, confirmed by measuring factor B and adding it back to restore AP50.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “TNF and LTA sit in the class I region” (✓ they are class III genes, in the inflammatory cluster between class I and class II); “C4A and C4B are functionally identical” (✓ four residues underlie their different target groups and lytic efficiency, and they generally carry different blood-group antigens); “Factor B loss must be lethal before birth” (✓ complete factor B deficiency has been reported in children and in one patient diagnosed in adulthood, and it does not impair growth or development).

cues.text: Trap one: TNF and LTA sit in the class one region. No: they are class three genes, in the inflammatory cluster between class one and class two.
Trap two: C4A and C4B are identical. No: four residues change what they bind and how well they lyse, and the two generally carry different blood-group antigens.

Trap three: losing factor B must be lethal before birth. No: complete factor B deficiency has been reported in children and in one patient diagnosed as an adult, and it does not impair growth or development.

props.title: ✗ “C4A = C4B.”
lines: ✓ Amino vs hydroxyl · Rodgers vs Chido

scenes.title: A for Amines, B for Bursting
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “C4A grabs Amines on Antigen–antibody complexes; C4B Binds hydroxyls and Bursts cells.” Tokens: A = amino groups, immune complexes · B = hydroxyl groups, haemolysis · Class III = the middle shelf. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: C4A grabs amines on antigen-antibody complexes. C4B binds hydroxyls and bursts cells. And class three is the middle shelf, between one and two.
Where it breaks: these are preferences, not absolutes, and the blood-group link is general, not fixed. Gene copy number varies between people, and the letters say nothing about Rodgers and Chido.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Class III (between I and II): C4A, C4B, C2, factor B, TNF, LTA”, “CH50 absent + AP50 normal → C2 · CH50 normal + AP50 absent → factor B”.

cues.text: The class III region between class I and class II carries C4A, C4B, C2, factor B and TNF, and an absent CH50 with normal AP50 points toward a classical-pathway gap such as C2 deficiency while a normal CH50 with absent AP50 points toward an alternative-pathway gap such as factor B.

explanation.what: Plain language: between the two antigen-presenting regions of the MHC lies a crowded stretch that holds several complement genes and the TNF gene. Because they sit so close, their variants are usually inherited together. Scientific terms: MHC class III region, C4A, C4B, C2, complement factor B (CFB), TNF, lymphotoxin alpha (LTA), copy-number variation, Rodgers and Chido antigens, complotype, CH50, AP50.
explanation.why: C4A and C4B differ at four amino acids, which shifts their preferred targets: C4A handles immune complexes better and C4B lyses more efficiently. Low C4 copy number and complete early-component deficiency predispose to SLE, while loss of an alternative-pathway protein such as factor B leaves a patient open to meningococcal and pneumococcal infection.
explanation.measure: Screen with CH50 (classical) and AP50 (alternative). CH50 <10% with normal AP50 → classical pathway (C1q, C1r, C1s, C4 or C2; a normal C4 level argues against C4). Normal CH50, undetectable AP50, normal C3 → factor B, factor D or properdin. Both undetectable → terminal pathway. Then measure individual components; reconstitution with the purified protein confirms.
explanation.differs: C4A (amino groups, immune complexes, Rodgers) vs C4B (hydroxyl groups, haemolysis, Chido); C2 deficiency (classical gap, often asymptomatic, SLE in a minority, pneumococcal infection) vs factor B deficiency (alternative gap, extremely rare, invasive meningococcal or pneumococcal infection).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: place TNF/LTA or a complement gene in the class III region, pick the C4 isotype by binding chemistry or blood-group antigen, or name the deficiency from a CH50/AP50 pattern.

mnemonic.text: C4A grabs Amines on Antigen–antibody complexes; C4B Binds hydroxyls and Bursts cells. Class III is the middle shelf.
mnemonic.explanation: Links each isotype letter to its preferred target and main strength.
mnemonic.limitation: Target binding and lytic strength are preferences, not absolutes; the Rodgers/Chido association is general, not fixed; copy number varies between people; the letters do not encode Rodgers or Chido.

CH50/AP50 cut-offs come from one reference laboratory; methods differ.
takeaway: The class III region between class I and class II carries C4A, C4B, C2, factor B and TNF, and an absent CH50 with normal AP50 points toward a classical-pathway gap such as C2 deficiency while a normal CH50 with absent AP50 points toward an alternative-pathway gap such as factor B.

questions.stem: A woman with arthritis, a photosensitive rash and recurrent pneumococcal pneumonia has CH50 below 10% of normal, a normal AP50, and normal C3 and C4. Which deficiency is most likely?

options.rationale: Correct. A classical-pathway gap with a normal AP50 and normal C4 fits C2 (or, less often, C1q/r/s); C2 deficiency is linked with SLE in a minority and pneumococcal infection.
Incorrect. Factor B deficiency abolishes AP50 while CH50 stays normal.
Incorrect. Terminal deficiencies make both CH50 and AP50 undetectable or low.
Incorrect. Complete C3 deficiency would show a very low C3 level, and here C3 is normal.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly contrasts the C4 isotypes?

options.text: C4A reacts preferentially with amino groups and generally carries Rodgers; C4B binds hydroxyl groups and generally carries Chido
options.rationale: Correct. This is the classic isotype difference.

options.text: C4A binds hydroxyl groups and carries Chido; C4B reacts with amino groups and carries Rodgers
C4A and C4B are functionally identical products of one gene
options.rationale: Incorrect. They are encoded by separate genes and differ at four amino acids that change their activity.

options.text: C4A is more efficient than C4B at lysing cells
options.rationale: Incorrect. C4B is the more efficient haemolytic isotype; C4A is better at processing immune complexes.

questions.stem: Where are the TNF and lymphotoxin alpha (LTA) genes located?

options.text: In the MHC class III region, between the class I and class II regions
options.rationale: Correct. They belong to the inflammatory cluster of the class III region.

options.text: In the MHC class I region with HLA-A, -B and -C
options.rationale: Incorrect. This is the classic trap; they are class III genes.

options.text: In the MHC class II region with HLA-DR and -DQ
options.rationale: Incorrect. Class III lies between class I and class II, and TNF/LTA are there.

options.text: Outside the MHC, on a different chromosome
options.rationale: Incorrect. They are inside the MHC on chromosome 6.

claims.text: Class III lies between class I and class II, is defined by position, ~700 kb, 61 genes, most gene-dense; contains C4A, C4B, C2, CFB, TNF and LTA.
Complotype: originally haplotypic combinations of MHC-linked complement gene variants; now also used system-wide.
C4A vs C4B: four residues at 1101–1106; amino vs hydroxyl groups; immune-complex processing vs haemolysis; Rodgers vs Chido; copy numbers; low copy number and C4 deficiency as SLE risk.
C2 deficiency: 28-bp deletion with exon 6 skipping; prevalence 1:10,000–20,000; >60% asymptomatic; SLE in 10–30%; pneumococcal infections; CH50 <10% with normal AP50.
Factor B deficiency: extremely rare, compound heterozygous cases, infections mostly meningococcal or pneumococcal, normal CH50 with undetectable AP50, normal development.

C4B 5–10× haemolytic activity; 35% with one C4 null allele; C4B*Q0 3.5-fold meningitis risk; C4A*Q0 homozygosity and SLE; SC01 and the ≥3-Mb extended haplotype; HSP70 in class III; no homozygous factor B deficiency ever described; C2 deficiency as the single most common complement deficiency.
claims.note: Reviewer figures not found in the open sources read, except that Macedo 2016 reports C2 deficiency as the most common deficiency in one ESID registry series of 77 patients, which is too narrow to teach as a general fact; not taught.

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 51 Hit 13 says homozygous factor B deficiency is “likely embryonic lethal”. Bougeard 2026 reports complete factor B deficiency (compound heterozygous loss-of-function variants) that does not impair growth or development, with one patient diagnosed in adulthood; the lesson teaches the source (register flag rv-factor-b-not-lethal).
Ch. 51 Hit 7 gives 2–4 C4 genes, exceptionally up to 6. Wang 2021 gives C4A 0–5 and C4B 0–4 copies with a highest total of 7; Macedo 2016 gives 2–8 (register flag rv-c4-copy-number).

Ch. 51 Hit 4 gives C2 deficiency as 1 in 10,000 with 20–40% SLE-like disease. Macedo 2016 gives homozygous prevalence 1:10,000–20,000 and SLE in about 10–30% (10% in its table) (register flag rv-c2-deficiency-figures).

Ch. 51 Hit 9 defines complotype only as the MHC complement haplotype (CFB, C2, C4A, C4B). Harris 2012 notes this was the original meaning but uses the term for complement variants across the whole system (register flag rv-complotype-scope).
